text:
The Army academy will be relocated to the central Chungcheong region, while the Navy and Air Force academies will be kept in place, the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) and the government said Wednesday, revising an earlier plan to merge them into a unified military college.
Wednesday's announcement finalizes a revision to the original plan to merge the three academies into a single institution, as the government sought to offer a compromise amid strong pushback from alumni groups, cadets and other stakeholders.
The revised plan retains the initial proposal to establish a joint academy at the Jaundae military complex in the central city of Daejeon, about 140 kilometers south of Seoul, but each armed service will keep their existing schools as a regional campus.
To do so, the Korea Military Academy — the Army college — will move out of Seoul and be relocated to a site in the central-western region of Chungcheong.
The Navy Academy and the Air Force Academy will stay in their current locations -- in the southern coastal county of Jinhae and the central provincial city of Cheongju, respectively.
"For specialized training during the second and third years, it is more efficient to keep the Navy and Air Force academies at their current locations, but we needed to find a new location for the Army academy," Rep. Kim Byung-joo told reporters after a policy coordination meeting between party and government officials.
The exact relocation site for the Army academy in the Chungcheong region has yet to be decided, Kim added.
The revised plan will adopt a so-called 1-2-1 model, where cadets complete shared coursework in their first and final years at the joint military academy and spend their second and third years for branch-specific training at their respective schools.
The revision also includes a plan to establish a new graduate school for master's and doctoral courses at the main campus to offer a path for in-depth military education, the defense ministry said in release.
The government plans to apply the new system to cadets entering in 2029, with each military branch continuing to recruit cadets separately until then to minimize confusion.
Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul expressed his commitment to establishing the combined academy to nurture creative talent capable of breaking away from conventional educational frameworks.
"By having Army, Navy and Air Force cadets train together and unite as a single warrior community, we will foster them into key leaders of our military capable of prevailing on any battlefield," Kang said during the meeting.
Kang also stressed the need to set a "clear and bold direction," while reviewing the implementation process in a "thorough and prudent" manner.
The new military academy will operate directly under the ministry, unlike the existing academies that fall under each individual armed service, the ministry said, citing the need for a "consistent and balanced" management and oversight in budget and other related policies.
The revised plan marks a retreat from an initial July proposal to merge the three service academies into a single institution inside the Jaundae compound and close down the existing schools.
Amid growing opposition to the plan, Kang, a retired Army general, had signaled an adjustment to the initial framework, highlighting that the move is not aimed at abolishing the three academies.
Alumni groups have denounced the planned integration as an attempt to weaken the core identity and capabilities of each military branch.
Army college graduates, in particular, have argued that it was a politically driven move by the Lee Jae Myung administration to curb the Army's influence over its involvement in past military coups and the short-lived martial law attempt by former President Yoon Suk Yeol in 2024.
